spb-birth.s: More than three hundred years ago, in 1703, Tsar Peter the Great wanted to build a new city by the sea. It was a hard place to build. There was wet, muddy land, the River Neva and a cold wind. First, people built a fortress on little Hare Island. It was called the Peter and Paul Fortress. That was how Saint Petersburg began.
a: With a fortress on Hare Island

spb-names.s: At first the city was called Saint Petersburg. Then its name changed to Petrograd, and later to Leningrad. In 1991 the city got its first name back. And people love it and just call it Piter.

spb-gun.s: There is a cannon in the Peter and Paul Fortress. Every day, at twelve o'clock exactly, it goes bang! It is not for war. It tells everyone the right time. Long ago, people in the city set their watches by this bang. The cannon has no cannonball. It just makes a loud bang.

spb-rider.s: By the River Neva stands a big statue of Peter the Great. The tsar sits on a horse, and the horse is standing up on its back legs. A French artist, Étienne Falconet, made it. Under the horse lies a huge rock, called the Thunder Stone. The rock was found in a forest. It took many months to bring it to the city over land and water. The statue is made of bronze. The poet Pushkin named it the Bronze Horseman.

spb-cats.s: The Hermitage is one of the biggest museums in the world. It is in the Winter Palace, where the tsars used to live, and in the buildings next to it. And real cats live in the Hermitage! More than two hundred and fifty years ago, the first cats came here to catch mice. Today the cats still look after the rooms under the museum. They even have a holiday of their own.

spb-bridges.s: Petersburg is built on islands, so it has a lot of bridges. From spring to autumn, some bridges go up at night. The two halves of the bridge lift up. Then big ships can sail along the Neva. The most famous one is the Palace Bridge. If you are on the far side too late, you must wait until the bridge comes down again.
a: So that ships can sail through
So that the bridges can rest
So that the fish can fall asleep

spb-nights.s: At the start of summer, Petersburg has white nights. The sun hides for just a short time. At night it is as light outside as in the evening. You can read a book outside without a torch. This is because the city is far in the north. But in winter there is very little daylight.

spb-peterhof.s: Peterhof is near Petersburg, by the sea. It is the summer palace of Peter the Great. It has more than a hundred and fifty fountains. The best thing is this: the fountains in the Lower Park have no pumps. The water runs down from the high hills through pipes. Then it shoots up into the air. There are trick fountains too. You walk along a path — and splash! You get wet!
a: The water runs down from the hills by itself
The water is carried in buckets

spb-isaac.s: It took forty years to build Saint Isaac's Cathedral. The man who planned it was a Frenchman, Auguste de Montferrand. The huge dome is covered with gold. On a sunny day it shines over the city. Each big column was cut from one block of granite, a hard stone. And from the high walkway around the columns, all of Petersburg lies below you, as if in the palm of your hand.

spb-chizhik.s: By the River Fontanka, on a ledge of the stone wall near a bridge, sits a tiny statue of a little bird. It is Chizhik-Pyzhik, the siskin. It is only as big as your hand, so it is hard to see. People say: throw a coin, and if it stays next to the siskin, your wish will come true. It is very hard to hit, but everybody tries!

spb-kunst.s: Peter the Great loved everything strange and new: stones, shells, old tools and odd things from different countries. For them he made the first museum in Russia: the Kunstkamera. The word means “a room of strange things”. The Kunstkamera has a tower. Long ago people watched the stars from a room in the tower.

spb-garden.s: The Summer Garden is the oldest garden in Petersburg. Peter the Great planned it too. Stone statues stand along the paths. There is also a statue of Ivan Krylov, who wrote fables. A fable is a short story about animals. Around him are the animals from his stories: the monkey with glasses, the crow, the fox and many more. Try to find them all!

spb-faberge.s: Carl Fabergé lived in Petersburg. He made jewellery. For the tsar's family he made Easter eggs from gold and shiny jewels. Inside each egg was a surprise: a tiny carriage, a little ship or a toy bird that could move. Today the eggs are in museums, and some of them are in Petersburg.

spb-angel.s: A tall golden tower with a pointed top stands above the Peter and Paul Fortress. It is part of the cathedral. For a long time it was the tallest building in the city. At the very top stands an angel with a cross. The angel keeps the city safe. Once the angel needed mending. The roof worker Peter Telushkin climbed up the tower with only one rope and no frame to help him!

spb-hermitage.s: The Winter Palace by the River Neva was once the home of the Russian tsars. It has more than a thousand rooms. If you went into a new room every day, it would take years! Empress Catherine the Second collected paintings. She kept them in a separate building next to the palace. That place was called the Hermitage. In French the word means “a quiet place to be alone”. Today the Hermitage is one of the biggest museums in the world. The Winter Palace is now part of it.
a: A quiet place to be alone

spb-peacock-clock.s: The Hermitage has an amazing clock called “The Peacock”. It is a golden tree. A peacock and a rooster sit on its branches. At the top, in a cage, there is an owl. The clock is more than two hundred years old, but it can still move! When it is switched on, the owl turns its head. The peacock spreads its beautiful tail. The rooster crows. The clock face is hidden in a mushroom cap under the tree.

spb-alexander-column.s: The huge Alexander Column stands on Palace Square. It was cut from one single piece of granite, a hard stone. An angel with a cross stands on top. Nothing fixes the column to the ground. It stays up because it is so heavy! More than a thousand soldiers and workers lifted it up with ropes. And it has stood there for almost two hundred years!

spb-kazan-cathedral.s: The Kazan Cathedral stands on Nevsky Prospect. Its columns curve out in a half circle. They look like two big stone arms hugging the square. There are ninety-six columns! Andrey Voronikhin planned the cathedral. He was an architect, a person who plans buildings. As a boy he was a serf, which means he was not free. But people saw how clever he was, and he became famous.

spb-spas-mosaic.s: The Church of the Saviour on Spilled Blood stands on the Griboyedov Canal. It has colourful domes that look like lollipops. Inside, almost all the walls and ceilings are covered with mosaic. A mosaic is a picture made from tiny pieces of coloured glass, like a huge jigsaw puzzle. From far away it looks painted, but it is glass! Skilled workers made these pictures over many years.

spb-mariinsky.s: The Mariinsky Theatre is one of the most famous theatres in the world. It was named after Empress Maria Alexandrovna. Inside, the hall where people sit is blue and gold. A huge hanging lamp shines under the ceiling. In 1892 the ballet “The Nutcracker” was shown here for the first time. Peter Tchaikovsky wrote the music. People still dance it here every winter, before the New Year.

spb-aurora.s: A real old warship stands by the Petrogradskaya Embankment. It is the ship “Aurora”. It was built in Petersburg and put on the water in 1900. It is easy to know: it has three tall chimneys. Aurora is the name of an old goddess of the sunrise. Today the ship is a museum. You can go up on deck, look at the guns and find out how the sailors lived.

spb-nevsky.s: Nevsky Prospect is the main street of Petersburg. It starts at the Admiralty. On top of the Admiralty's tall tower there is a little golden ship that shines. The street is four and a half kilometres long. On the way it crosses the River Moyka, the Griboyedov Canal and the River Fontanka on bridges. It ends at the Alexander Nevsky Lavra. The street got its name from it.

spb-anichkov-horses.s: The Anichkov Bridge goes over the Fontanka, right on Nevsky Prospect. At its corners stand four bronze statues. Each one shows a young man taming a fiery horse. An artist called Peter Klodt made them. He loved horses very much. During the war the statues were taken down. People carefully buried them in a garden nearby to keep them safe. Afterwards the horses came back to their places.

spb-lion-griffin-bridges.s: Two narrow little bridges with animals go over the Griboyedov Canal. On the Lion Bridge, four lions sit. They hold chains in their mouths, and the bridge hangs from the chains. On the Bank Bridge sit griffins. They are animals from fairy tales, with a lion's body and wings. The griffins' wings are golden! You can only walk on these little bridges.

spb-fontanka.s: The River Fontanka flows through the middle of Petersburg. Long ago it did not even have a real name. People called it Bezymyanny Yerik, which means “a stream with no name”. Then people made the Summer Garden with its fountains nearby. The water for the fountains came from this little river. That is how the river became the Fontanka. Today people go for boat trips on it.
a: It gave water to the fountains

spb-new-holland.s: New Holland is an island shaped like a triangle. It appeared when people dug canals around it. Logs for ships were kept and dried there. It was named after Holland, where Peter the Great learned to build ships. On the Moyka side you can see a huge stone arch. Boats used to sail through it into the island. Today there is a park here. In summer everybody lies on the grass, and in winter people go ice skating.

spb-rostral-columns.s: Two red columns stand at the tip of Vasilyevsky Island. The front parts of ships stick out of them. They are called rostra, so the columns are called the Rostral Columns. Long ago a fire burned on top to show ships the way. Now the fire is lit on holidays. At the bottom sit stone giants. People say they are the rivers Volga, Dnieper, Neva and Volkhov.

spb-sphinxes.s: Two sphinxes lie by the Neva, near the Academy of Arts. A sphinx is a lion with a human head. These are real, from Ancient Egypt! They were cut from granite, a hard stone, more than three thousand years ago. Their faces look like the Egyptian king Amenhotep the Third. The sphinxes came to Petersburg by ship across the sea. Now they look at each other across the Neva.

spb-botanic-garden.s: Peter the Great started the Botanical Garden in 1714. At first people grew herbs for medicine here, so it was called the Apothecary Garden. Now palms and flowers from hot countries grow in its glass greenhouses. The most famous plant is the cactus “Queen of the Night”. Its huge white flower opens at night. By morning it fades. So that everyone can see it, the garden is sometimes open at night!

spb-elagin.s: Yelagin Island is a big green park with no cars. You can walk along the paths, go out in a boat and feed the squirrels. The island is named after one of its owners, Ivan Yelagin. At the west end of the island, on a narrow strip of land, sit stone lions. People love to watch the sun go down into the Gulf of Finland from here.

spb-kronstadt.s: Kronstadt is a city on Kotlin Island, in the middle of the Gulf of Finland. You can get there by car along a dam, a long wall in the water. You can even drive through a tunnel under the water. In Kronstadt, on a bridge, there is a copper plate with a little line on it. It is the footstock, a mark for the level of the sea. In Russia, the height of mountains and the depth of seas are measured from it. So all the measuring in Russia starts here!
a: The height of mountains and the depth of seas

spb-amber-room.s: The blue Catherine Palace stands in Tsarskoye Selo. The Amber Room is inside it. The walls are covered with amber. Amber is the hard, golden sap of trees that grew very long ago. A king of Prussia gave this room to Peter the Great many years ago. In the war it vanished, and nobody has ever found it. So skilled workers spent more than twenty years making it again. Now it shines once more, like honey in the sun.

spb-pavlovsk-squirrels.s: Pavlovsk is a small town near Petersburg. It has a huge park and a palace. The main animals living in the park are squirrels! They are not afraid of people at all. Hold out your hand with a nut on it, and keep still. A squirrel may jump down from a tree and take the nut from your hand. But the nuts must have no salt and must not be roasted. That is better for squirrels.

spb-gatchina.s: The Birch House stands in Gatchina Park. From outside it looks like a pile of firewood. But inside there are lovely rooms hidden! It was a surprise gift from his wife to Paul, who later became Emperor. And a path under the ground goes from Gatchina Palace to Silver Lake. There is a little cave there called “Echo”. Shout, and it answers you!

spb-oranienbaum.s: Oranienbaum is an old palace with a park, by the Gulf of Finland. In German, its name means “orange tree”. In the time of Catherine the Second, people built a Rolling Hill here. Guests sat in little carts and raced down a long slope. The hill is gone now, but a pretty little house is still there. And in Portugal such rides are still called “Russian mountains”!

spb-smolny.s: The blue and white Smolny Cathedral stands by the Neva. It looks like a fancy cake. Its name comes from the Russian word “smola”, which means tar. Tar is a sticky black stuff. In the time of Peter the Great there was a Tar Yard here. Tar was kept there for ships, so that they would not leak. Later the Smolny Institute opened nearby. It was one of the first schools for girls in Russia.

spb-metro.s: The Petersburg metro is one of the deepest in the world. It had to be built far down under the ground. Above it there is wet, soft ground, rivers and canals. The deepest station in Russia is “Admiralteyskaya”. It is eighty-six metres down. That is almost like a building with thirty floors, but going down! That is why the escalators here are very long.

spb-lakhta.s: A glass tower stands in Lakhta, on the shore of the Gulf of Finland. With its pointed top it is four hundred and sixty-two metres tall. It is the tallest building in Europe. The tower twists up like a flame. On a clear day you can see it from many parts of the city. Right next to it is the Gulf of Finland. In summer you can run about on the sand and watch the sunset.
a: In Lakhta, by the Gulf of Finland
On the roof of the Hermitage

spb-h-domik.s: When the city was just starting, people built a small wooden house for Tsar Peter the Great. Soldiers who were also carpenters built it in just three days! The logs were painted to look like bricks. Peter lived in it in summer and looked out of the windows at the Neva. The little house is still there today. A stone house carefully covers it from above, like a jewellery box.

spb-h-plotnik.s: Peter the Great wanted Russia to have its own navy, which means its own warships. He went to Holland. He got a job as an ordinary carpenter at a shipyard, a place where ships are built. People there called him Peter Mikhailov. With the best craftsmen he built a real ship. In Petersburg, Peter made a big shipyard, the Admiralty. He often picked up an axe himself and worked next to the shipbuilders.

spb-h-botik.s: When Peter was a young man, he found a little boat with a sail in an old barn. It was a botik, from another country. A Dutch craftsman mended the botik, and Peter learned to sail in it. That was how he began to love the sea. Many years later Peter brought the botik to Petersburg. He sailed it along the Neva himself, with big ships sailing behind. Since then people call the botik “the grandfather of Russian ships”. After all, everything began with it.

spb-h-assamblei.s: In 1718 Peter the Great thought up parties called “assemblies” in Petersburg. These were happy evenings in the houses of important people. Guests danced, talked, and played chess and draughts. Women were invited too. That had never happened in Russia before. Peter came to these evenings himself and danced with everyone.

spb-h-ekaterina.s: Empress Catherine the Second loved paintings very much. In 1764 she bought more than two hundred paintings at once from a trader from Berlin. She kept her treasures in a place called the Hermitage. It is a French word. It means “a quiet place to be alone”. At first only the empress and her guests saw the paintings. Now her collection has grown into a huge museum for everyone.

spb-h-licej.s: In 1811 a lyceum, a school for boys, opened in Tsarskoye Selo near Petersburg. One of the first pupils was twelve-year-old Sasha Pushkin. His friends called him “the Frenchman”, because he knew French very well. At a test, Pushkin read his poems to the old, famous poet Derzhavin. Derzhavin was so happy that he wanted to hug the young poet. But the boy ran away because he felt shy.

spb-h-mendeleev.s: Everything around us is made of tiny bricks called elements. Iron, gold and oxygen are elements. A scientist from Petersburg, Dmitri Mendeleev, put them in order in one table. For some he left empty squares. He said: they will be found one day! A few years later, scientists really did find these elements. A huge Mendeleev table is on the wall of a building on Moskovsky Prospect.

spb-h-pavlov.s: The scientist Ivan Pavlov studied how our bodies work, and dogs helped him. He noticed something. If the same sound always plays before food, a dog soon waits for a treat when it hears the sound. For his discoveries Pavlov was the first person in Russia to win the Nobel Prize. He was very thankful to the dogs. He asked for a statue of a dog to be put up in Petersburg.

spb-h-lomonosov.s: Mikhail Lomonosov was a scientist and a poet. He learned how to make coloured glass, called smalt. To get the colours he wanted, Lomonosov tried thousands of tests. With his helpers he made pictures from small pieces of smalt. These pictures are called mosaics. His big mosaic about Peter the Great's win at Poltava is on the stairs in the building of the Academy of Sciences in Petersburg.

spb-h-pavlova.s: Anna Pavlova was born in Petersburg. One day her mum took her to the theatre to see the ballet “The Sleeping Beauty”. Anya said later that from that day she only dreamed of dancing. She went to a ballet school and became a famous ballerina. The dance “The Swan” was made for her. She travelled all over the world with it. A light, sweet cake was even named after her: “Pavlova”.

spb-h-chajkovskij.s: Peter Tchaikovsky loved music from the time he was little. But he was sent to Petersburg to study law. He finished school and got a job as an office worker, sorting papers all day. But he could not stop thinking about music. Then the first music school in Russia opened in Petersburg. Tchaikovsky became one of its first students. He left his job and became a composer, a person who writes music. Now the whole world knows him.

spb-h-navodnenie.s: The Neva flows into the sea, the Gulf of Finland. In autumn, a strong wind from the sea sometimes pushes the water back into the river. Then the Neva spills over its banks. This is called a flood. Some houses have marks on their walls. The water once rose up to that line. The biggest flood was in 1824. Today a dam in the gulf, a big wall in the water, keeps the city safe. Its gates close when the water gets high.

spb-h-ledohod.s: All winter the Neva is covered with thick ice. In spring the ice cracks and breaks into big pieces. They float away to the sea. People call this the ice drift. Long ago, when the river was free of ice, the chief of the Peter and Paul Fortress brought the tsar a cup of Neva water. It was a sign: the river is free, and ships can sail again.

spb-h-koryushka.s: In spring, when the ice melts, a little silver fish called smelt swims into the Neva from the Gulf of Finland. It has a funny smell. It smells of fresh cucumbers! In spring smelt is sold all over the city. People fry it and eat plates and plates of it. In May, St Petersburg even has a smelt festival. For people in St Petersburg, this little fish is a sure sign of spring.

spb-h-parusa.s: Every summer St Petersburg has a party for young people who have finished school. It is called “Scarlet Sails”. Scarlet means bright red. At night a ship with scarlet sails floats along the Neva, and fireworks boom in the sky. The name comes from a book by Alexander Grin. In the book, a girl called Assol waited for a ship with scarlet sails, and her dream came true.

spb-h-krasin.s: In 1928, in the cold Arctic, the airship “Italia” crashed onto the ice. The travellers were left on a big piece of ice in the middle of the sea. They painted their tent red so that aeroplanes could see it. The icebreaker “Krasin”, a ship that breaks ice, came to help. It broke through the thick ice and reached the people. The icebreaker saved them. Now it stands by the river bank in St Petersburg, and you can climb aboard.
a: So it could be seen from aeroplanes

spb-h-tramvaj.s: Long ago, a horse tram ran along the streets of St Petersburg. It was a little carriage pulled by horses. And in winter an electric tram ran on the ice of the Neva! The rails were laid right on the ice. The posts for the wires were frozen into it. The ice tram ran every winter from 1895 to 1910. Electric trams came to the city streets later.
a: On the ice of the Neva

spb-h-doroga.s: During the war, enemy soldiers closed in around Leningrad. The city was trapped in a ring. This is called a siege. Almost no food could get into the city. In winter the big Lake Ladoga froze, and people made a road across the ice. Lorries with flour and bread drove along it. On the way back they took away children and sick people. People called it the “Road of Life”, because it saved so many.

spb-h-begemot.s: During the siege, a hippo called Beauty lived in the Leningrad Zoo. Hippos need a lot of water, or their skin gets dry and cracks. But no water came to the zoo any more. So the keeper, Evdokia Dashina, took forty buckets of water on a little sledge every day. She warmed it up and washed Beauty. The hippo lived through the siege and for many more years.

spb-h-dozhd.s: St Petersburg is by the sea, so the air is wet and there are lots of clouds. It rains often, so people in St Petersburg are used to taking an umbrella. The weather changes fast. In the morning the sun shines, and by the afternoon it is already raining a little. But after the rain the wet streets shine. You can see the houses and lamps in the puddles. A sunny day here is like a little holiday, and everyone goes out for a walk at once.

spb-h-chajki.s: St Petersburg is by the sea, so many gulls live in the city. They build nests right on the roofs of houses. They make a lot of noise in the morning. There are also many hooded crows here. They are grey, but their head, wings and tail are black. Crows are very clever and hide food for later. Sometimes you can see a gull and a crow arguing over a bit of bread roll.

spb-h-dvor.s: In old St Petersburg the houses stand close together, shoulder to shoulder. Inside them are hidden yards with tall walls on all sides. Stand in the middle and look up. The sky looks like a tiny square, as if you were at the bottom of a well. That is why such yards are called well courtyards. Through some yards you can walk from one street to another.
a: The sky looks small, as if seen from a well
Everyone drinks from a bucket there

spb-h-slova.s: In St Petersburg some things have their own names. The stone edge of the pavement is a porebrik here. In Moscow it is a bordyur. The entrance hall and stairs of a block of flats are called a paradnaya in St Petersburg, not a podyezd. White bread here is just a bulka, and shawarma is called shaverma. With words like these, you can tell at once who is from Petersburg.

spb-h-pyshki.s: People in St Petersburg love pyshki. They are soft little rings of dough, fried in hot oil. They are covered with lots of icing sugar, so it is easy to get it on your nose. In Moscow, rings like this are called ponchiki. In St Petersburg they are only pyshki. There are little shops called pyshechnye. They have fried pyshki there for many years. They serve them with cocoa or sweet milky coffee.

spb-rusmuseum.s: The yellow and white Mikhailovsky Palace stands in the middle of St Petersburg. The Russian Museum is inside it. It keeps only paintings by Russian artists. The museum opened in 1898. “The Ninth Wave” by Aivazovsky hangs here, with a huge sea wave. So does “The Last Day of Pompeii” by Bryullov. In front of the palace there is a little park. A statue of Pushkin stands there, reading poems with his arm raised.

spb-engineers-castle.s: Emperor Paul the First dreamed of living in a real fortress. So Mikhailovsky Castle was built for him. People dug deep ditches full of water all around it. You could only get in over drawbridges, bridges that lift up. Later the castle became a school for future engineers, and it was called the Engineers' Castle. And very close by, at the Fontanka, sits a tiny bronze bird, Chizhik-Pyzhik.

pt-king.s: Cascais was a small fishing village. One day the King of Portugal, Luís the First, chose it for a summer holiday by the sea. The king's family lived in an old fortress, the Citadel. Important guests came after the king. That is how the fishing village became a famous place for holidays.

pt-light.s: In 1878 the first electric light in Portugal was switched on in Cascais. It was put up in the Citadel for Prince Carlos's birthday. Just think: everywhere else there were only candles and oil lamps, and here was a bright electric light! Everyone who saw it was very surprised.

pt-boca.s: Near Cascais there are cliffs with a huge cave and an arch. This place is called Boca do Inferno, which means “Hell's Mouth”. It sounds scary, but it is very beautiful there. In a storm the waves crash into the cave, boom, and throw water high into the air. It sounds as if a huge monster is roaring.

pt-farol.s: The Santa Marta lighthouse stands in Cascais, right by the water. It is white with blue stripes, like a sailor's striped shirt. At night the lighthouse shines for the ships, so they do not hit the rocks. Inside the lighthouse there is now a museum. It tells about the lighthouses of Portugal.

pt-roca.s: Cabo da Roca is the furthest west you can go on the land of Europe. After it there is only the ocean, all the way to America. Tall cliffs drop straight down to the waves. The Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote about a place like this: “Here the land ends and the sea begins.” These words are carved on a monument there.

pt-pena.s: The Pena Palace stands right on top of the Sintra mountains. It looks like a palace from a fairy tale. It has yellow and red little towers and castle walls with notches on top. King Ferdinand the Second built it. He loved art very much. All around is a huge park with lakes, little caves and trees from all over the world. In fog it looks as if the palace is floating in the clouds.

pt-belem.s: The stone Belém Tower stands in Lisbon, by the River Tagus. It is five hundred years old. Sailors set off from here for far-away countries. Look closely, and you can find a stone head of a rhinoceros on the tower. Once a real rhinoceros was brought to Lisbon from India. People never forgot it!

pt-gama.s: Long ago people were looking for a way to India by sea. They wanted spices: pepper, cinnamon and cloves. In 1497 Vasco da Gama set off from Lisbon with his ships. He sailed all the way around Africa. The trip was long and dangerous. But in 1498 he reached India! That is how Portugal became a land of great sailors.

pt-azulejo.s: In Portugal many houses have painted tiles on them. They are called azulejos. Most often the tiles are white and blue, but they can be many colours. Whole pictures are made from little squares: ships, flowers and scenes from everyday life. The tiles also keep the walls safe from heat and wet.

pt-tram.s: An old yellow tram, number 28, runs along the narrow little streets of Lisbon. Lisbon is built on hills. The tram zooms up and rolls down. The streets are so narrow that the tram almost touches the houses. And the tram goes ding-ding!

pt-ocean.s: Lisbon has one of the biggest aquariums in Europe. In the middle there is a huge tank, like a piece of the open ocean. Sharks, rays and the funny sunfish swim there. Sea otters live there too. They love to swim on their backs.

pt-nata.s: The most famous Portuguese tart is the pastel de nata. It is a crisp little basket filled with soft, sweet custard. Monks who lived in a monastery in Belém made it first. When the monastery closed, the recipe was sold to a shop next door. They still bake the tarts there today. Only a few people know the secret recipe.

pt-regaleira.s: In Sintra, in the old garden of Quinta da Regaleira, there is a strange well. It has no water in it. A stone staircase winds down and down in a circle. The well is deep, about as deep as a building with nine floors. It looks like a tower turned upside down. From the bottom you can see a small circle of sky. Paths under the ground lead from the bottom to little caves and to a lake with a waterfall.

pt-mouros.s: The walls of the Moorish Castle stand on top of the mountain above Sintra. The Moors built it more than a thousand years ago. The walls, with notches along the top, go over the rocks, up and down, like a long stone snake. You can walk along them and climb the towers. From the top you can see the colourful Pena Palace, the town of Sintra and, on a clear day, even the ocean.

pt-monserrate.s: Monserrate park is not far from Sintra. More than a hundred and fifty years ago an Englishman wanted to bring plants here from all over the world. Now palms grow here, and tall sequoia trees from America, and ferns as tall as trees. In the middle of the park stands a palace with domes and stone patterns like lace. It looks like something from a fairy tale. Walking here is like visiting lots of countries in one day.

pt-guincho.s: Guincho is a big beach not far from the middle of Cascais. A strong wind from the ocean often blows here. That is why kitesurfers come. A big kite pulls them, and they race over the waves on a board. The wind also carries sand, and the sand piles up into sandy hills called dunes. A wooden path goes along the dunes, so you can walk without stepping on the plants.
a: A little motor in the pocket

pt-pescadores.s: In the very middle of Cascais there is a small beach, called the Fishermen's Beach. Cascais was once a fishing village, and fishermen still live here. Their boats rock in the bay. On the shore the fishermen mend their nets. Fresh fish is taken to the market, where local people and cooks buy it. At this beach you can look at the colourful boats and the folded nets.

pt-carmona.s: Marechal Carmona park is in Cascais. Peacocks, hens and cockerels walk freely along its paths. A peacock can suddenly open its tail like a huge fan with eyes. Ducks swim in the pond, and turtles sit in the sun on the stones. The birds are not afraid of people at all, so you can see them very close.
a: Sit in the sun on the stones

pt-nazare.s: In winter, the town of Nazaré gets the biggest waves that people surf on. Some are as tall as a building with lots of floors! It is all because of a huge deep valley, a canyon, at the bottom of the ocean. It helps the waves grow. Brave surfers race along these waves. People watch them from a high cliff. A little fortress with a red lighthouse on its roof stands there.
a: A canyon at the bottom of the ocean

pt-obidos.s: Óbidos is a small town with a tall stone wall all around it. Long ago King Dinis gave this town to Isabel, who was going to be his wife, as a wedding present. After that, Óbidos was given to the queens of Portugal for many years. You can walk along the top of the wall around almost the whole town. You can look down at the white houses with flowers. Just hold a grown-up's hand tight. There are no rails!

pt-mafra.s: In the town of Mafra there is a big palace. Inside is an old library with thousands and thousands of books. At night, bats fly there. They are the library's guards! They catch little beetles and moths that could spoil the old pages. In the evening the workers cover the tables with cloths. In the morning they wash the floor. That is how the little helpers look after the books.

pt-ponte-porto.s: In the city of Porto, the iron Luís the First bridge crosses the River Douro. It has two floors! On the top floor the metro train goes, and people walk. On the bottom floor cars drive, and people walk too. An engineer who used to work with Gustave Eiffel planned the bridge. Eiffel made the famous tower in Paris. From the top floor you can see the whole old town and the boats on the river.

pt-rabelo.s: Long ago, wooden rabelo boats sailed on the River Douro. They have a flat bottom, a big square sail and a very long oar at the back. The oar helps the boat to turn. The boats carried heavy barrels down the river. The barrels came from the valley where grapes grow. Now the rabelos stand by the bank, across from old Porto. In summer, on Saint John's day, people race them.

pt-coimbra.s: In the city of Coimbra there is one of the oldest universities in the world. It stands on top of a hill. Above it rises a tower with a clock and a bell. The students call the bell “the Goat” as a joke. Its ringing called students to lessons. Many students here still wear long black capes, like in an old fairy tale.

pt-moliceiro.s: The city of Aveiro is by the water. Long moliceiro boats sail along its canals. Long ago, people used these boats to collect seaweed and water grass from the bottom of the lagoon. They put it on the fields to help plants grow. The front and back of each boat have bright pictures painted on them. Often they are funny little scenes with words. Now the moliceiros take visitors for rides, and you can look at the pictures on the way.

pt-evora.s: In the middle of the city of Évora stand the tall stone columns of an old temple. The Romans built it almost two thousand years ago. Back then this land was part of their huge country. The columns are made of granite, a hard stone. Their carved tops are made of white marble. People often call it the temple of Diana, goddess of the hunt, but nobody knows for sure who it was for.

pt-benagil.s: In the south of Portugal, in the Algarve, there is a cave called Benagil. The sea made it in the golden rock. There is a round hole in the roof, like a little window. A ray of sunlight falls in through it. You cannot walk to the cave. You go there by sea, in boats and kayaks. From the top of the cliff, you can look into the window and see sand and water below.

pt-levadas.s: On the island of Madeira it rains a lot in the north and a little in the south. So long ago, people cut narrow channels in the mountains. They are called levadas. Water runs along them from the rainy side of the island to the fields and gardens. Paths run beside the levadas, and now people walk on them. The path goes through a forest of moss and ferns, and the water bubbles along beside you.

pt-sete-cidades.s: In the Azores there is a huge bowl that an old volcano left behind. The place is called Sete Cidades. Two lakes lie in the bowl. One looks blue and the other looks green. A little bridge goes between them. A legend says a princess and a shepherd cried and made the lakes. They had eyes of different colours. Scientists say the colours come from how deep the water is and what grows in it.

pt-baleias.s: Many whales and dolphins live in the ocean near the Azores. Sperm whales are huge whales with a big square head. You can see them here all year round. On the shore stand little stone tower houses. Long ago people built them to hunt whales, but hunting whales has not been allowed for a long time. Now watchers look out from the towers with binoculars. They look for fountains of water over the sea. Then they tell the tourist boats where to go.

pt-cegonhas.s: Lots of white storks live in the Alentejo, in the south of Portugal. They build huge nests of sticks on posts, chimneys and bell towers. Many storks do not fly away to Africa for the winter now. They stay in Portugal. By the ocean, storks even build nests on the cliffs above the waves. You can hardly see this anywhere else in the world.

pt-cortica.s: The cork oak grows in Portugal. Its bark is very thick and soft. Once every nine years, people carefully take off some of the bark. The tree keeps on growing. Then they paint the last number of the year on the trunk. That way they remember when they took the bark. People make corks, mats and even shoes from the bark. Portugal gets more cork than any other country.

pt-santa-justa.s: Lisbon is built on hills, and it is hard to climb the steep streets. So more than a hundred years ago, people built the Santa Justa Lift in the middle of the city. It is a tall iron tower with patterns like lace. The lift takes people from the street below up to a little bridge. The bridge goes to the next hill. At first the lift worked with a steam engine. Later it worked with electricity.

pt-ponte-abril.s: The long red Twenty-Fifth of April Bridge goes across the River Tagus in Lisbon. It looks a lot like the famous Golden Gate Bridge in America. Cars drive on the top, and trains go below. When cars roll over the iron grid of the bridge, you hear a hum, as if the bridge is singing. On the other side of the river stands a big statue of Christ with open arms. It is called Cristo Rei. You can go up it in a lift.
a: A hum, like the bridge is singing

pt-sao-jorge.s: On a hill in the old centre of Lisbon stands the Castle of Saint George. Peacocks walk around freely in its gardens. In one of the towers there is a dark room with a magic camera. Mirrors and glass show the whole city right now on a big dish: cars, ships on the river and people in the streets. From the castle walls you can see the River Tagus and the red roofs of the houses.

pt-jeronimos.s: In the Belém part of Lisbon stands the huge pale Jerónimos Monastery. People began to build it when Portuguese sailors were finding new sea ways far away. That is why there are sea ropes, knots and shells carved in stone on its walls. In the inner yard, the columns are covered with fine patterns, like lace. It looks as if the stone has become soft, like dough.

pt-golfinhos.s: Not far from Lisbon, near the city of Setúbal, the River Sado flows into the ocean. A group of bottlenose dolphins lives there all year round. There are only a few dozen of them. Scientists know each one by the shape of the fin on its back. In Europe it is very rare for dolphins to stay in one place like this. From a boat you can see the dolphins come up to take a breath of air.
a: By the fin on its back
By the number on its tail

pt-c-henrique.s: People called Prince Henry the Navigator. But he never went on long sea trips himself. He sent ships further and further south, along the coast of Africa. For this, people built caravels. They were light ships with triangle-shaped sails. They could sail in a zigzag, even against the wind. Sailors were afraid of Cape Bojador, and people told scary stories about it. But in 1434 Captain Gil Eanes sailed round the cape, and the way south was open.

pt-c-dias.s: In 1488 Captain Bartolomeu Dias sailed his ships south along Africa. A big storm pushed them far out into the ocean for many days. When the wind calmed down, Dias saw that he had already gone round the bottom of Africa! On the way back, the sailors saw a tall, rocky cape. They called it the Cape of Good Hope. Now there was hope of sailing round Africa to India.

pt-c-magellan.s: Ferdinand Magellan was born in Portugal, but the Spanish king gave him the ships for the trip. In 1519 Magellan's five ships sailed west. Near South America he found a narrow path of water. Today it is called the Strait of Magellan. Beyond it the ocean was calm, and Magellan named it the Pacific, which means “peaceful”. Three years later one ship, the “Victoria”, came home. That is how people sailed all the way round the Earth for the first time.

pt-c-afonso.s: The first king of Portugal was Afonso Henriques. He was a brave fighter, and people called him the Conqueror. In 1143 the king next door agreed that he was a king, and Portugal became its own country. In the town of Guimarães an old wall says: “Here Portugal was born.” The borders of the country have hardly changed for more than seven hundred years.

pt-c-romans.s: Two thousand years ago the Romans ruled this land. They called it Lusitania, and Lisbon was Olisipo. The Romans built roads, bridges and houses with floors made of tiny coloured stones. In the city of Évora the columns of a Roman temple still stand. And the Portuguese language grew out of Latin, the language of the Romans.

pt-c-arabic-words.s: Many hundreds of years ago, the Moors lived in the south of Portugal. They were Arabs and Berbers from North Africa. They left hundreds of words in the Portuguese language. “Azeite” is olive oil, “arroz” is rice, and “açúcar” is sugar. All these words came from Arabic. The name Algarve is Arabic too. It means “the west”. When a Portuguese person says “oxalá”, they hope that something will come true.

pt-c-earthquake.s: On the first of November, 1755, a terrible earthquake shook Lisbon. Many houses fell down. Then a huge wave came from the sea, and fires started in the city. A minister led the building of the new city. Later he became the Marquis of Pombal. The new streets were straight and wide. In the walls of the houses, builders hid a wooden frame. It stopped the houses from falling down in new earthquakes.

pt-c-pombal.s: After the big earthquake, the Marquis of Pombal built the middle of Lisbon all over again. He made the streets straight. He gave many of them to different workers who make things by hand. That is how Gold Street, Silver Street and Shoemakers' Street came to be. These names are still there today. The Marquis himself stands on a tall column in the square with his name. A lion stands beside him.

pt-c-camoes.s: Luís de Camões is the most famous poet in Portugal. When he was young, he was a soldier, and he lost an eye in a battle. He wrote a long poem called “The Lusiads”. It is about the Portuguese sailors. People say his ship once sank, and Camões swam to the shore. He held his poem above the water. On the tenth of June, Portugal Day, people remember Camões too.

pt-c-carnations.s: For many years, strict rulers ruled Portugal. People could not say what they thought. On 25 April 1974 soldiers came out onto the streets of Lisbon to change that. A woman gave a soldier a red carnation. He put the flower into his gun. Other people did the same. Almost no shots were fired. Today this day is a holiday of freedom.

pt-c-brazil.s: In 1500 the sailor Pedro Álvares Cabral sailed to Brazil. There he saw a tree with wood as red as fire. In Portuguese it is called “pau-brasil”. The name of the country comes from it. Today many more people speak Portuguese in Brazil than in Portugal. People also speak it in Angola, Mozambique and other countries.
a: After a tree with red wood

pt-c-obrigado.s: In Portuguese, boys and girls say "thank you" in different ways. A boy says "obrigado". A girl says "obrigada". The word means something like "I am thankful to you". Until lunchtime, Portuguese people say "Bom dia!" to each other. In the evening they say "Boa noite!" Try saying these words in a café or a shop.

pt-c-orange.s: Portuguese sailors brought sweet oranges to Europe from Asia. That is why in many countries the orange has a name that comes from Portugal. In Greek it is “portokali”, in Turkish “portakal”, and in Bulgarian “portokal”. The Russian word “apelsin” means “Chinese apple”. The Portuguese call the orange “laranja”.

pt-c-calcada.s: Pavements in Portugal are often made of small stones, white and black. This is the calçada, the Portuguese pavement. The workers lay each little stone by hand and tap it into place with a hammer. The stones make pictures of waves, little ships and flowers. In Rossio Square in Lisbon the stones make waves, like the sea. The same waves were later made on the famous Copacabana beach in Brazil.

pt-c-galo.s: There is an old story about the town of Barcelos. A traveller there was said to have stolen something, but he had not. The judge was eating a roast rooster for his dinner. The traveller said: "If I did nothing wrong, this rooster will stand up and crow!" And the rooster jumped up and crowed loudly, "cock-a-doodle-doo". The traveller went free. Now the painted rooster is a sign of Portugal.

pt-c-santo-antonio.s: Saint Anthony was born in Lisbon. In June the city celebrates his day with great joy. On the night of 12 to 13 June people grill sardines in the streets. They eat them on a piece of bread. There are bright decorations, music and dancing everywhere. People give each other basil in a little pot, with a paper flower and a short rhyme. Parades in fancy dress go down the big street. They come from the different parts of the city.

pt-c-bacalhau.s: Bacalhau is cod fish that has been salted and dried. People catch the cod far away in the cold northern seas. Then they salt it and dry it, so it stays good for a long time. Before cooking, they leave the fish in water for a day or two. The Portuguese say there are more bacalhau recipes than days in the year. They call it “the faithful friend”. On Christmas Eve many families eat bacalhau with potatoes and cabbage.

pt-c-water-dog.s: The Portuguese water dog is a great helper for fishermen. It has curly fur and skin between its toes, like a duck. Long ago these dogs dived for nets and fish that fell in the water. They even swam from boat to boat, or to the shore, with notes. Once there were almost no dogs like this left, but people who love dogs saved them. Dogs like this even lived with an American president.

pt-c-lusitano.s: Lusitano horses are an old kind of horse from Portugal. They are named after Lusitania, the name the ancient Romans gave to this land. The Romans loved how fast the horses were here. They even told a story that the baby horses here were children of the west wind. Lusitanos are brave, calm and quick on their feet. To music they can do beautiful steps, as if they were dancing.

pt-c-eusebio.s: Eusébio was born in Africa, in Mozambique. As a child he kicked a ball in the streets. Then he came to Lisbon and became one of the best footballers in the world. He was so fast and so good that people called him “the Black Panther”. In 1965 he won the “Ballon d'Or”. It is the prize for the best footballer in Europe. At the 1966 World Cup, Eusébio scored more goals than anyone.

pt-c-ronaldo.s: Cristiano Ronaldo was born in 1985 on the island of Madeira, in the city of Funchal. When he was twelve, he went to Lisbon on his own to learn football. He missed home very much, but he kept on training. In 2016 Portugal's team, with Ronaldo, became the champions of Europe. Now the airport on Madeira has his name.
a: At the North Pole, among the walruses
On the roof of a bus

pt-c-carnival.s: At the end of winter, before Lent, Portugal has a carnival. Children wear costumes to school. Happy parades go through the streets. In the town of Torres Vedras, men dress up in dresses and wigs. In the village of Podence, people run around in masks and shaggy clothes made of bright wool. Bells jingle on their belts. That is how they say goodbye to winter with lots of noise.

pt-c-bolo-rei.s: At Christmas in Portugal, people bake bolo-rei, the “king's cake”. It is round, with a hole in the middle, like a crown. On top it has fruit covered in sugar, and nuts, like jewels. An old tradition says a dried bean was hidden in the cake. Whoever finds the bean must buy the cake next year. People eat bolo-rei until the sixth of January, Kings' Day.
a: Crow like a rooster three times

pt-c-chestnuts.s: In autumn the streets of Portugal smell of roasted chestnuts. The sellers roast them on their carts, and white smoke curls up above them. On the eleventh of November, Saint Martin's Day, families and schools have a chestnut party. An old story says Martin gave half of his cloak to a freezing poor man. Just then the sun came out. That is why warm days in November are called “Saint Martin's summer”.
a: His umbrella with flowers on it

pt-espichel.s: Not far from Lisbon is Cape Espichel, with high cliffs above the ocean. On one cliff you can see big round holes in a long line going up. They are footprints of dinosaurs that walked here millions of years ago. Back then the rock was soft mud. People used to think they were the tracks of a giant mule from an old story. But scientists found out that dinosaurs with long necks, who ate plants, walked here.

pt-flamingos.s: Near Lisbon, the River Tagus gets very wide, with lots of shallow water. Every year thousands of pink flamingos fly in. They stand on one leg. They put their beaks in the water upside down to sift out food. Flamingos are pink because of their food: tiny shrimps and tiny water plants. It is best to watch the birds quietly through binoculars, so you do not scare them.
a: Their food: tiny shrimps and tiny water plants

mu-nutcracker.s: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky is a great Russian composer. He studied at a music school in Saint Petersburg. His ballet “The Nutcracker” is a fairy tale about New Year's night. In it we meet a girl called Masha, the brave Nutcracker and the evil Mouse King. In the “Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy” you hear the celesta. It is an instrument like a little piano with bells inside. Tchaikovsky found it in Paris. He kept it secret until the first show.

mu-album.s: Tchaikovsky wrote twenty-four pieces for the piano for his little nephew Volodya. Together they make the “Children's Album”. It has “The Doll's Illness”, “The New Doll”, “March of the Wooden Soldiers” and even “Baba Yaga”. Children who learn music still play these pieces today.

mu-bee.s: When he was young, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov was an officer in the navy. For almost three years he sailed on a warship across seas and oceans. Then he became a composer and a teacher at the music school in Saint Petersburg. In his opera “The Tale of Tsar Saltan”, Prince Gvidon turns into a bumblebee. The music of the “Flight of the Bumblebee” is so fast that it sounds like a bumblebee buzzing by your ear: bzzz!

mu-peter.s: Sergei Prokofiev wrote a musical fairy tale for children called “Peter and the Wolf”. Each character has its own instrument. The little bird is the flute, the duck is the oboe, the cat is the clarinet, and grandfather is the bassoon. Three horns play the wolf. The violins and other strings play Peter. You listen and know who is who by the sound!

mu-pictures.s: The composer Modest Mussorgsky had a friend, the artist Viktor Hartmann. When his friend died, there was a show of his drawings. Mussorgsky walked through it and wrote music about the pictures. It has “The Hut on Hen's Legs”, “Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks” and “The Bogatyr Gates”. Between the pictures you hear “Promenade”. That is the composer himself, walking from picture to picture.

mu-glinka.s: Mikhail Glinka is called the father of Russian classical music. He wrote an opera from Pushkin's fairy tale “Ruslan and Lyudmila”. In it the evil wizard Chernomor takes Lyudmila away, and the brave Ruslan saves her. Chernomor is a tiny old man with a huge beard, and all his strength is in his beard!

mu-mozart.s: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart lived in Austria. He began to write music when he was only five years old! At six he was already playing for an empress. Little Mozart could even play on keys covered with a cloth. In his life he wrote more than six hundred pieces of music.

mu-beethoven.s: Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer. When he grew up, he began to lose his hearing. In time he could not hear at all. But he kept writing music, because the music sounded inside him. That is how he wrote the Ninth Symphony with the “Ode to Joy”. The whole world knows this tune, and you can even play it on a toy piano.

mu-vivaldi.s: The Italian composer Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, so people called him “the Red Priest”. He wrote four pieces for violin and orchestra: “Spring”, “Summer”, “Autumn” and “Winter”. In “Spring” birds sing and little streams splash. In “Summer” a thunderstorm roars. In “Winter” the violins shiver, as if teeth were chattering from the cold.

mu-bach.s: Johann Sebastian Bach lived in Germany more than three hundred years ago. He played the huge organ in a church. An organ has hundreds of pipes. Some are tiny, as small as a pencil. Some are huge, taller than a house with two floors. You play the organ with your hands and even with your feet! Bach had many children, and several of them became composers too.

mu-fado.s: In Lisbon people sing fado. These are sad, beautiful songs about the sea, about faraway trips and about missing home. A Portuguese guitar plays along with the singer. It has a round body like a pear, and twelve strings. People love fado so much that its songs are on a list of treasures that belong to everyone in the world.

mu-shost.s: Dmitry Shostakovich was born and lived in Saint Petersburg. In the war, enemies were all around the city, and people were hungry and cold. Shostakovich began to write his Seventh Symphony there. He wrote it for his home city. In the summer of 1942 it was played in Leningrad, and the radio sent the music out. People listened and felt: our city will not give up.
